title: Condign vs congruous merit: all grant free gift; some call living faith congruous
source_text: XLVI. Porro per meritum de condigno intelligunt opus cui merces ex justitia debetur, per meritum autem de congruo opus cui nihil quidem debetur ex justitia, sed quod a bonitate divina aliquid impetrat, cuique decet bonitatem & aequitatem divinam aliquid tribuere. Itaque consentiunt Doctores omnes Ecclesiae Romanae peccatorum remissionem, & justificationem hominis peccatoris esse donum Dei gratuitum, & ex justitia non deberi fidei. Quod vero dicunt eorum nonnulli fidem illam mereri de congruo, per hoc non aliud significatum volunt, quam fidem quae per dilectionem operatur peccatorum veniam & justificationem a bonitate divina impetrare, & congruum esse divinae bonitati & sapientiae, ut peccatorem, qui fide efficaci per bona opera, ad misericordiam Dei in Christo confugit, a peccatis absolvat & justitia donet.
pass_a_gloss: Further, by merit de condigno they understand a work to which a wage is owed from justice; but by merit de congruo a work to which nothing indeed is owed from justice, but which obtains something from divine goodness, and to which it befits divine goodness and equity to give something. Therefore all the Doctors of the Roman Church agree that the remission of sins and the justification of a sinful man is a free gift of God, and is not owed to faith from justice. But when some of them say that that faith merits de congruo, by this they mean nothing else than that faith which works through love obtains from divine goodness pardon of sins and justification, and that it is fitting to divine goodness and wisdom that he absolve from sins and gift with righteousness the sinner who by efficacious faith through good works flees to God's mercy in Christ.
pass_b_english: Condign = wage from justice; congruous = fitting gift from goodness—no debt.
All Rome: first justification is free gift; 'congruous merit of faith' only means living faith fittingly obtains pardon.
